claims.text: Untreated W–Cu composites containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments exhibit phase separation and interfacial void formation.
A nanoscale nickel coating should be applied to the tungsten phases before composite fabrication.
Pre-coating the tungsten phases with nickel will suppress phase separation at W–Cu interfaces.
Pre-coating the tungsten phases with nickel will suppress interfacial void formation.
The nickel coating will form a continuous thin interlayer at the tungsten–copper interface.
A nickel interlayer improves wettability between tungsten and copper.
A nickel interlayer improves interfacial bonding between tungsten and copper.
A nickel interlayer reduces the effects of thermal-expansion mismatch during processing and irradiation.
A nickel interlayer reduces chemical-potential differences during processing and irradiation.
Improved wettability and bonding, together with reduced mismatch and chemical-potential differences, minimize interfacial voids and phase separation.
Reducing interfacial voids and phase separation will enhance the effective thermal conductivity of the composite.
The nickel-coated W–Cu composite will have significantly higher effective thermal conductivity than an untreated composite processed and tested identically.
The nickel-coated W–Cu composite will retain a more stable interface than the untreated composite under high heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The intervention is applicable to consolidation by sintering or hot isostatic pressing.
The intervention is applicable at processing temperatures and irradiation levels typical of joints between plasma-facing and cooling components.
Effectiveness may be limited when processing conditions exceed the thermal stability of the nickel layer.
Irradiation-induced phase changes may limit the effectiveness of the nickel interlayer.
